extracted.intended_audience: district court judges, magistrate judges, and patent litigators (case managers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judicial case management of patent litigation focused on early-stage procedures (discovery, claim construction, motions, damages, multi-defendant cases) to reduce cost and complexity and promote early resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require cooperation and communication before court discovery disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Require parties to meet and confer (at least telephonically) before bringing discovery disputes to the court; provide stern warnings concerning cooperation and communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps to plan for Markman hearing, reduces need for court intervention to resolve discovery disputes, and generally improves forward progress of the case and ensures claim-construction and summary judgment motions will be informed. The court may require leave to bring discovery disputes (e.g., via telephonic hearing or brief letter exchange).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit number of discovery disputes without prior leave
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider limiting the number of discovery disputes the court will entertain without prior leave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduces the burden of repetitive discovery applications and preserves court resources; can be paired with requirement of telephonic monitoring or short-letter exchanges prior to formal motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt or adapt patent local rules
rubrics_metrics.description: If the district does not have its own patent local rules, consider adopting the patent local rules of another district (e.g., Northern District of California) and discuss with parties how such rules might be adapted to the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using established patent local rules can improve efficiency and eliminate common discovery disputes; customization with parties can tailor rules to case-specific needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan Markman hearing logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan for the Markman (claim construction) hearing, including scope of tutorial and whether to have live testimony from experts or other witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early planning for tutorial and testimony informs claim-construction and summary-judgment readiness and can guide discovery scope and scheduling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss timing and relationship of summary judgment to claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss the timing of summary judgment motions and their relationship to claim construction, and identify any other issues that could potentially give rise to dispositive motions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether claim construction must precede summary judgment and whether potential dispositive issues require much discovery. Early analysis can shape schedule and avoid premature or tardy motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict number of summary judgment motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss any restrictions that the court will or might impose on the number of summary-judgment motions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits can greatly affect parties' strategies and practices; see guidance in § 6.1 for summary-adjudication best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate summary judgment from motions in limine
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss how the court will distinguish motions for summary judgment and motions in limine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifying distinctions reduces premature consideration of in limine motions and tardy consideration of summary judgment motions, streamlining pretrial practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate mediation into case-management
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss approaches to mediation, appoint a mediator, or initiate a mediator selection process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes mediation as an integral and continuous part of the litigation process, encourages cooperation on information exchange, and enhances the chance of early resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify basis for including multiple defendants early
rubrics_metrics.description: In multidefendant litigations, identify at an early stage the patentee’s basis for including multiple defendants in the litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early identification of the rationale for joinder helps the court efficiently manage the case and decide whether joinder is appropriate under current law (e.g., post-AIA, In re EMC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage multidefendant cases based on standards compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: When multidefendant litigation is based on compliance with industry standards, recognize that discovery regarding functional specifications can often be fairly limited, but anticipate complicated SSO-related defenses and counterclaims (e.g., noncompliance with SSO policies, FRAND issues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such cases may implicate equitable, contract-based, and antitrust claims and defenses; confidentiality and damages concerns may counsel bifurcating damages from liability; identifying the standards-based nature at outset can significantly narrow fact discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage customer/manufacturer multidefendant litigations
rubrics_metrics.description: When plaintiffs sue manufacturers and their customers (OEMs, distributors), the court should consider staying claims against customer defendants pending resolution of manufacturer claims, and be mindful of third-party discovery and protective-order issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customers are often superfluous; courts frequently stay customer suits or require customers to consent to be bound by judgments. Manufacturers may intervene or file declaratory-judgment actions; first-to-file and customer-suit-exception analyses (judicial efficiency) often determine outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address spoliation and preservation issues early
rubrics_metrics.description: Because spoliation (destruction of documents) can spawn satellite litigation, the court should address preservation and spoliation accusations early in the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly prevalent where plaintiffs are NPEs with few documents and defendants have many; early handling can curb resource-draining disputes. See § 4.4.2.1 for analyzing spoliation as the case progresses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use early, targeted claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Require parties to identify claim terms which, if construed, could dispose of a significant portion of the case and proceed to construe those terms on an expedited schedule (sometimes with shorter briefs and without expert discovery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some courts (e.g., E.D. Tex.) have used this to encourage early resolution when plaintiffs appear to seek nuisance settlements; expedited claim construction can prompt early settlements or dismissals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct defenses susceptible to early dismissal
rubrics_metrics.description: Inequitable conduct defenses may be susceptible to early motion to dismiss due to heightened pleading standards (see Exergen, Therasense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inequitable conduct is eliminated early, discovery can be narrowed significantly; apply Federal Circuit standards on pleading and proof of materiality and intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter (§101) is amenable to early resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent eligibility under § 101 (abstract ideas, laws of nature) can often be addressed early via motion to dismiss or summary judgment, especially for simple business methods or broad claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex inventions may require claim construction, background tutorials, and factual development; factual disputes over inventive application may implicate subsidiary factual determinations (Teva) and may warrant awaiting discovery/tutorial before deciding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrajurisdictional/extraterritoriality issues can be resolved early
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims based on extraterritorial conduct (e.g., §§ 271(f), 271(g), 271(b)) often involve ascertainable facts about a defendant’s contacts with the U.S. that could lead to early resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early fact-finding on contacts can narrow or dispose of claims alleging foreign conduct as infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willfulness may be susceptible to early resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Willfulness requires proof of both objective and subjective elements (In re Seagate); early evidence may objectively demonstrate no willful infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early adjudication of willfulness can narrow discovery and focus the case; courts should look for evidence that objectively negates willfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early disposition of indirect infringement claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect infringement claims (and willfulness) require that the accused infringer knew of the asserted patents prior to litigation and are therefore susceptible to early determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In method-claim cases, indirect-infringement theories often depend on whether a single entity is responsible for all claimed steps (Limelight, Muniauction); absence of control/direction or multiple noninfringing uses can be fatal early on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require early damages contentions
rubrics_metrics.description: Require the patentee to provide damages contentions that (1) identify types of damages sought (lost profits, reasonable royalty, or both), (2) explain specific theories and methodologies intended to value infringement, and (3) identify a range within which its ultimate damages number for each accused instrumentality is expected to fall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To enable meaningful disclosures, require accused infringer to produce financial documents related to the accused instrumentalities; such early contentions allow parties to challenge legal and factual bases for damages earlier and promote proportionality under Rule 26(b)(2)(C)(iii). Examples: preliminary damages disclosures (Judge Bencivengo), initial-disclosure damages model (Judge Sue Robinson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accelerated damages discovery schedules (including Track B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider accelerated schedules for damages-related fact and expert discovery (e.g., complete damages discovery months before other fact discovery and serve damages expert reports shortly thereafter); consider placing cases on expedited tracks like Eastern District of Texas Track B with early good-faith damages estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An accelerated schedule permits earlier Daubert resolution, allows a limited 'do-over' if exclusion occurs without moving trial, and supports proportional discovery limits (Track B limits interrogatories/RFPs absent leave). Table 2.9 summarizes example Track B deadlines (infringement contentions, initial disclosures, good-faith damages estimate, invalidity contentions, readiness notice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define 'do-over' policy for damages expert reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish clear ground rules for allowing a party to rectify or substitute a damages report, addressing timing and scope of permitted revisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because preparing damages reports is costly and critical, a do-over policy surfaces likely disputes and signals risks of questionable methodologies; courts should discuss timing and scope and consider whether a one-time correction is permitted if exclusion occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early consideration/vetting of Daubert challenges on damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Set an early schedule for consideration of Daubert challenges or vet core damages theories early, leaving room for narrower challenges after discovery and final expert reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vetting damages theories earlier helps avoid last-minute Daubert disputes; examples show mixed success but can allow courts to set parameters on acceptable damages methodologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider bifurcation or reverse bifurcation of liability and damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Depending on circumstances and settlement opportunities, consider bifurcating liability and damages or trying damages first when damages may be modest and liability complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bifurcation can streamline proceedings and tailor discovery; see § 8.1.1.3 for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider independent or court-appointed damages experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts might appoint a neutral damages expert under Fed. R. Evid. 706 to present their own report or comment on parties’ experts to address disparate and confusing economic testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A neutral expert can unmask problems early and offer insurance against speculative damages theories, though it adds costs and requires defining role and compensation; courts have used neutral experts in complex economic matters, but caution exists (examples of courts striking parts of court-appointed reports).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss timing and nature of damages disclosures at case-management conference
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should discuss with parties the timing and nature of damages discovery and damages-related Daubert proceedings at the case-management stage to avoid relegating damages disputes to the end of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early discussion clarifies parties’ damages positions, encourages settlement by clarifying the damages playing field, and preserves practical options for resolving Daubert and other disputes without crippling trial preparation.
